title: How to make a high-quality game with AI
author: dentegza
selftext:
I started making this game before AI blew up in 2022. It took so long because I'm a coder/screenwriter with no design skills, so I had to learn everything from scratch. Initially the story was told entirely through chat messages, but as AI evolved, I gradually incorporated more and more visuals into the game. Here's the AI stack I've used: Seedance 2.0 for cutscenes, Nano banana for images, and ElevenLabs for voice acting. The first thing I want to share with you is that music and voice acting are currently what AI does best, you can achieve amazing results with just a couple of regenerations. But unfortunately visuals is a completely different story.  
  
I've been working with generative AI since its early days, and I've come to a couple of conclusions based on my own experience. First of all, the more input you provide the better results you'll get. Instead of writing a vague prompt without any reference, give AI something to work with so it can understand the composition you're trying to build. E.g. you can manually draw sketches and ask AI to enhance them (add colors, shades, volume and so on) - this is how I've made characters for my game. Or you can just attach a real photo and ask it to redraw it in your chosen art style. This way, you can save tons of time and avoid regenerating a single image 100 times, hoping the next attempt will finally give you what you want.  
  
Second of all, do not expect AI to generate image with huge amount of details. If you try, you'll most likely get a result with tons of artifacts. The more details there are in a single image, the less attention AI seems to pay to each individual detail, resulting in sloppy stuff like messed-up faces in a crowd. In order to prevent it, you have to decompose the image into multiple parts and generate each one separately, then just combine them manually using some image editing tool.  
  
And lastly, regarding video generation, don't even try to write a prompt on your own - you'll get awful results. In order to get the most out of Seedance, you need to use the most powerful LLM models to build the prompt, I personally use either Fable or Opus 5.5 (they're quite similar so it doesn't really matter).  
  
That's basically it. Good luck to everyone making their games! Hope y'all find your audience and succeed.  
  
P.S. if you're interested in the game I've made, it's called "[Phantom: Hidden Sins](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4632330/Phantom_Hidden_Sins)", it's currently in pre-release on Steam, with a demo available.
